preferences.title: Readable technical language
preferences.summary: Use technically accurate language that remains readable without becoming simplistic.
preferences.body: Explain what is happening, why it matters, and what changes next. Keep useful technical detail, but replace opaque internal phrasing and unexplained implementation jargon with clear operational language.

preferences.title: Attack-centric reusable memory
preferences.summary: Prioritize reusable technology, version, vector, procedure, failure, and recovery knowledge over transient target identity.
preferences.body: Organize reusable knowledge around matching technology stacks, exact versions, attack vectors, procedures, scripts, prerequisites, observed outcomes, failed approaches, hazards, and recovery steps. Keep target names and addresses only as private provenance when they are required for traceability.

preferences.title: Titanium visual identity
preferences.summary: Use a sophisticated titanium, precision-engineered technology identity across Ti-Scale.
preferences.body: Favor high-contrast titanium materials, precise geometry, sharp Swiss editorial composition, and an advanced corporate technology aesthetic. Retain the established Ti-Scale typography. Avoid green as the defining titanium color and avoid generic cyberpunk decoration.

preferences.title: Light interface with dark titanium Brain
preferences.summary: Keep the main product light while presenting the Brain graph in a dark titanium theme.
preferences.body: Use an off-white, minimalist main application surface with precise single-pixel gray dividers and no decorative grid background. Integrate central artwork into the page rather than placing it on a separate white plate. Use a dark titanium graph workspace so the brain structure, nodes, and neuron signals remain visible and legible.

preferences.title: Sophisticated mechanical and particle motion
preferences.summary: Use advanced mechanical assembly, exploded-view, transformation, and particle motion with an accessible reduced-motion alternative.
preferences.body: Motion should make the product feel like an advanced engineered system: components assemble and disassemble with physical purpose, paginated or staged transitions transform the central form into interface modules, hover states react coherently, and graph activity resembles controlled neuron signals. The loading experience should use particle formation rather than a generic spinner. Reduced-motion mode must preserve meaning without spectacle.

preferences.title: Application-owned controls
preferences.summary: Use controls whose interaction and visual language belong to Ti-Scale rather than native operating-system menus.
preferences.body: Dropdowns, menus, buttons, selectors, and overlays should use accessible Ti-Scale components with consistent titanium styling, keyboard operation, focus behavior, and deterministic states.

preferences.title: Native iOS and Android delivery later
preferences.summary: Treat native iOS and Android applications as later delivery targets after the platform is ready.
preferences.body: Preserve domain and API boundaries that support future native mobile clients. Do not silently replace the current web delivery or claim native packaging is complete before dedicated compilation and validation on the target platforms.

preferences.title: High autonomy within enforced policy
preferences.summary: Prefer end-to-end autonomous progress when authorization, readiness, and safety policy permit it.
preferences.body: Minimize routine operator interruption after a valid Autonomous contract launches. This preference never expands authorization, weakens action policy, bypasses evidence requirements, or overrides a mandatory safe stop.

preferences.title: Evidence-first explanations
preferences.summary: Anchor explanations, classifications, failures, and recommendations in inspectable evidence.
preferences.body: State what was observed, what it supports, confidence, important uncertainty, and the next justified action. Keep raw output available for inspection, but do not present raw logs as verified evidence or make unsupported success claims.

preferences.title: Standalone Ti-Scale product
preferences.summary: Build and present Ti-Scale as an independent product rather than an embedded interface.
preferences.body: Ti-Scale should own its product identity, application boundary, runtime contracts, data lifecycle, release process, and documentation. Integration adapters may be explicit, but the product must not be framed or delivered as a skin inside another application.

preferences.title: Dedicated public source repository
preferences.summary: Maintain Ti-Scale in its own public source repository with an independent release history.
preferences.body: Keep Ti-Scale product code, release automation, issues, and version history in a dedicated public repository. Do not mix unrelated application source trees into that repository.

preferences.title: Professional standalone documentation
preferences.summary: Write Ti-Scale documentation as a complete, professional, self-contained product guide.
preferences.body: Documentation should explain Ti-Scale on its own terms, cover installation, operation, architecture, security, testing, and recovery, and avoid using another repository or running application as the narrative reference point.

preferences.title: Quality-first compatible model selection
preferences.summary: Prefer the highest-quality currently available compatible model when a model choice materially affects the result.
preferences.body: Prioritize result quality over choosing a cheaper or weaker model by default. Resolve choices from current capabilities and health, while still enforcing provider disclosure, authorization, tool compatibility, data policy, mission budgets, and reproducibility requirements.

preferences.title: Brain-shaped knowledge graph
preferences.summary: Arrange the memory graph as two connected hemispheres and a spinal structure formed by graph points and links.
preferences.body: The graph itself should form the brain anatomy rather than relying on hemisphere or spinal background images. Use small, legible titanium points, a restrained dot-based legend, optional slow rotation, and visible neuron-like signal paths after selection. Keep the canvas grid-free, make controls readable in the dark theme, and honor reduced motion.

preferences.title: Faceted titanium interface modules
preferences.summary: Shape panels and controls as parts of one coherent titanium machine rather than generic rectangular cards.
preferences.body: Use faceted, architectural module geometry that rhymes with the central titanium form. Buttons should feel like precise white-and-titanium HUD controls, panels should have subtle hovering or field-reactive movement, and transitions should assemble or release modules with mechanical continuity without harming readability.

preferences.title: Explicit evidence-backed attack outcomes
preferences.summary: Classify reusable attack knowledge by success, failure, supporting context, or unclassified state using canonical evidence.
preferences.body: Retain both successful and failed approaches when they teach a reusable condition. A success or failure label must come from a canonical terminal attempt and supporting evidence rather than prose inference. Failure memory should capture side effects, instability, repeated resets, unsafe ordering, required health checks, recovery steps, and the conditions that could make a later retry valid.

preferences.title: Private source linkage for every imported memory
preferences.summary: Keep every imported artifact and reusable memory linked to its originating engagement records through private provenance.
preferences.body: A reusable script, procedure, observation, failure, recovery, or artifact must expose an inspectable private provenance path to its source engagement, run, evidence, file hash, and original timestamp where available. Keep transient target names and addresses out of reusable content, but do not sever the private traceability needed to audit where the knowledge came from.

preferences.title: Dedicated operator-preference memory
preferences.summary: Retain explicit durable operator preferences in a distinct, user-controlled Operator Profile category.
preferences.body: Store explicit, durable, non-sensitive collaboration and product preferences only after operator confirmation. Make each preference inspectable, correctable, scopeable, exportable, expirable, and forgettable. Do not convert one-time commands, target details, credentials, sensitive traits, or safety-bypassing requests into reusable preference memory.

preferences.title: Active connected Obsidian Second Brain
preferences.summary: Use a real, health-verified Obsidian-compatible Vault as a synchronized human-readable view of the Second Brain.
preferences.body: Do not present a decorative or inactive Vault as connected. Connection status should require a real round-trip filesystem health check. Keep the canonical database transactional, synchronize the Vault incrementally with stable IDs and links, expose conflicts, and keep private provenance and reusable knowledge boundaries intact.

preferences.title: Audited Brain context for every agent
preferences.summary: Require commanders and specialists to retrieve the smallest relevant Brain context before meaningful work.
preferences.body: Planning, assignment acceptance, tool selection, attack attempts, phase changes, recovery, finding validation, reporting, and lesson proposals should use persisted, scope-safe Context Packs. Show which confirmed memories influenced the result. Brain context may improve behavior but must never override authorization, disclosure, evidence, or safety policy.
